assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks are a direct embodiment of the view that progress is limited by how precisely we can measure. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the lattice light shift while keeping Lamb-Dicke confinement, and Ye's strontium clocks reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 with huge atom numbers and long coherence. The result opened precision tests of relativity, searches for varying constants and dark matter, relativistic geodesy and a prospective redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori's magic-wavelength idea and early Sr lattice work, and Ye's demonstration of record accuracy and stability, are the decisive contributions. A two-person prize is natural and the supplied credit supports it. Other groups (e.g. at PTB, NIST, SYRTE) contributed important work, but the core conceptual and experimental lineage is clear.
assessment.maturity: Mature: independent confirmation across many laboratories and species (Sr, Yb, Hg), clock comparisons at the 1e-18 level and international roadmaps toward redefining the second. Recognition is timely and the field is stable.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would see this as too close to the 2005 and 2012 clock-related prizes (frequency comb, ion control); my recollection of the precise uncertainty record values is from memory, not verified here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: X-ray free-electron lasers created a new measurement instrument, with femtosecond coherent X-ray pulses that allow time-resolved structure and spectroscopy of matter at atomic scales. The impact spans AMO physics, condensed matter, chemistry and structural biology. The key physics (SASE, high-gain FEL theory, the electron-beam and undulator concepts) is original and clearly demonstrated by LCLS and FLASH.
assessment.attribution: The SASE concept and high-gain theory are associated with Pellegrini and Kim, and Rossbach with the TESLA/FLASH route to the first soft X-ray FEL. The set is plausible but the allocation among accelerator physicists, and the experimentalists and facility builders (LCLS, DESY, SACLA) who made it work, is not fully clean. I cannot confirm from the supplied text who is decisive.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: several operating facilities worldwide, widely used, extensive independent results, and recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Attribution is contested between theory proposers and machine builders; whether the prize would be seen as physics versus accelerator engineering; credits come from the supplied list, not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED brought strong light-matter coupling to superconducting circuits, giving controllable, readable qubits with long coherence and the architecture behind most current superconducting quantum processors. From an experimentalist's view, dispersive readout and the transmon-resonator platform are measurement techniques that turned a clever idea into a reliable device.
assessment.attribution: Blais and collaborators wrote the 2004 proposal, and Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling in the same year. The three-name set is coherent. Closely related transmon and Josephson-circuit work (Devoret, Martinis, Clarke recognised in 2025) may complicate how this is framed.
assessment.maturity: Mature in terms of demonstrations; the platform is widely replicated and drives industrial efforts. Recognition would be timely, although the 2025 Nobel for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits partly overlaps.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize and with transmon-qubit credit (Schoelkopf group, Koch et al.); whether the committee wants another superconducting-circuit award so soon.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and Blatt's experimental realisation of gates, entanglement and algorithms established a leading platform for quantum computation, with the highest gate fidelities and long coherence times. It is a clear case of theory converted into careful experiment.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the scheme and Blatt demonstrated the gate and scaled the platform. Other key experimentalists (Wineland and Monroe groups, with Wineland already recognised in 2012) and the Innsbruck versus NIST priority sharing leave some allocation questions, but the three names are a defensible configuration.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed by many groups and by commercial devices; recognition is reasonable and timely, though the quantum-computing field is still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize for ion control; B044 is a near-duplicate entry with the same names, so this ballot assumes the trapped-ion framing; whether Monroe or Wineland-group credit is missing from the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical addressing and coherent control of single colour-centre spins (NV centres in diamond, and others in SiC) allow room-temperature quantum sensing, single-spin readout and solid-state qubits and memories. Close to my own field of solid-state spins in crystals, I value that this has produced actual sensors (magnetometry, nanoscale NMR, bio-sensing) as well as quantum-information demonstrations.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated single NV optical detection of magnetic resonance, Awschalom extended control to multiple materials and ultrafast coherent manipulation, Walsworth developed magnetometry and imaging. Lukin's contributions are also large but would make a fourth name, so a three-person set must leave out significant contributors, and the allocation is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature for sensing and spin control, with extensive confirmation across groups; practical impact is expanding but commercial maturity is still partial.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over many groups (Lukin, Hanson, Jelezko, Wrachtrup, Awschalom), so any three-person set is debatable; the compound discovery mixes sensing and quantum-network aspects that may deserve separate recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Solid-state femtosecond lasers (Ti:sapphire, Kerr-lens mode-locking, SESAMs) made ultrafast pulses reliable, compact and widely accessible, and underpin spectroscopy, frequency combs, attosecond science and micromachining. The instrument-level impact on measurement is large and a good fit with the instrumentation tradition I value.
assessment.attribution: Moulton developed Ti:sapphire, Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking, and Keller invented SESAM mode-locking. These are distinct, individually decisive steps, so a three-way split is plausible, but the relative weight of each is open.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: decades of use and a ubiquitous technology, though recognition may feel late and overlapping with prior ultrafast and CPA prizes (Mourou/Strickland 2018, attosecond 2023).
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2018 and 2023 prizes; whether Kerr-lens mode-locking priority (Sibbett group) is clean; I am relying on recollection of the invention history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices have become quantum simulators in which Hubbard models are realised with tunable parameters and single-site readout (quantum gas microscopes), as shown by the superfluid to Mott insulator transition. This is an important new way to observe many-body physics with exquisite control.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, Greiner and Bloch demonstrated the Mott transition and microscope work. Because Greiner's and Bloch's lineages differ and others (Hänsch, Esslinger, Bakr, Gross) contributed, the allocation is not entirely clean, and Cirac is omitted if Zoller is chosen.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and widely replicated, but the simulation payoff for problems unsolved classically is still developing, so full impact may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Some overlap with the 2001 BEC and 2012 prizes; whether quantum simulation has yet solved an open problem; choice among Cirac and Zoller.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays, built from optical-tweezer arrays and blockade interactions, deliver defect-free 2D and 3D arrays with high-fidelity gates and quantum simulation, including exploring exotic phases and early error-corrected logical qubits. The experimental control is impressive and the field is moving very fast.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and collaborators supplied the proposals (Rydberg gates), Browaeys and Lukin led key demonstrations (arrays, simulation, logical processors); Saffman and others, with a fourth credited name, would also be strong. Three names cannot capture all decisive contributions, and the division between tweezer technology and Rydberg interaction work is unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Premature: rapid development, with the most important results (large-scale programmable processors) only a few years old, and independent confirmation still accumulating.
uncertainties: Maturity and independence of confirmation; allocation of credit among Browaeys, Lukin, Saffman and Zoller; tweezer technology credit (Ashkin, Grangier, Regal and Ni) is outside the supplied names.
